problem: The sentence 'the other four are either slow, destructive or accidental' lumps light triggering with the unwanted ones. Light triggering is a deliberate, precisely timed method used in HVDC valves, so a student may conclude light turn-on is always an accident or a fault.
fix: Say instead that the other four are either unwanted (thermal leakage, dv/dt), stressful to the device (forward breakover) or need a separate optical source (light), while only gate triggering gives cheap electrical control of the exact instant.

problem: 'when the control switch closes, the capacitor discharges into the gate through a resistor' is vague. Most exam RC trigger circuits have no switch at all: the capacitor charges through R from the supply and dumps its charge into the gate-cathode path when the circuit conditions allow, giving one sharp gate current spike per cycle.
fix: Describe it as: C charges through R; when the capacitor voltage is high enough the capacitor discharges through the gate-cathode junction (often via a series resistor and a blocking diode), giving a short gate pulse; the R-C also shifts the firing angle in AC controllers.

problem: 'A 1.05 W pulse in a 0.25 W resistor can still fail if the pulse is long or repeated fast' is loose: the resistor rating is an average (continuous) rating, so a short pulse above it is normally safe and failure comes from average power or pulse energy, not from the peak alone.
fix: Say: the 0.25 W figure is a continuous average rating; check average power = peak power x duty ratio, and also check the resistor's short-pulse energy rating when the pulse is long or repeated fast.
